context_blurb:
Light from a distant galaxy is old light, and it carries a record. Its stretched waves show how the universe has grown, a faint glow from every direction shows how hot it once was, and the speeds of stars and galaxies reveal ingredients that no one has yet identified.

Each dark line in a galaxy's spectrum marks one exact colour, so astronomers can see every line slide toward red. Light's waves stretch as space expands, so waves that arrive twice as long as they set out mean the distances between galaxies have doubled since the light left. The universe was then half its present size. Dust can redden a galaxy's colour, but only a true red shift moves the lines.

In 1948 Robert Herman and Ralph Alpher reasoned that the hot young universe George Gamow pictured must have left a faint afterglow. It set out some 380,000 years after the beginning, from gas near 3,000 degrees above absolute zero. They expected it to arrive at only about five degrees above absolute zero, because the universe's expansion has stretched its light. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the glow by chance, as faint microwaves.

Fred Hoyle, who rejected the Big Bang to the end, called the glow starlight that dust had absorbed and given out again. In 1989 the COBE satellite put that to the test: John Mather's team measured the glow's brightness wavelength by wavelength. A blackbody, an object that soaks up all light falling on it, glows in one smooth curve set by its temperature alone, and the glow matched one such curve almost perfectly. Dust lies near and far, some warmer and some cooler, and dust at many temperatures would blend many curves into a mix no single curve fits.

A second COBE instrument, led by George Smoot, compared the glow's temperature across the sky. In 1992 his team found spots warmer or cooler than average by only some thirty millionths of a degree. Theorists had expected such ripples because galaxies had to grow from slightly denser patches, which gravity drew together over billions of years.

By calculation, the first minutes made matter about one part in four helium by mass, the rest hydrogen. Stars turn hydrogen into helium too. So astronomers test the forecast in glowing gas clouds in small galaxies with hardly any heavy elements, because stars have added the least helium to them. There helium is about 24.5 percent of the mass, close to the forecast.

In 1933 Fritz Zwicky used red shifts measured by Milton Humason and Edwin Hubble to time the galaxies darting about inside the Coma Cluster. At about a thousand kilometres a second, they moved far too fast for the gravity of its visible stars to hold them. Zwicky concluded that far more matter is there than can be seen, and he called it dark matter. Modern studies agree.

In 1970 Vera Rubin and Kent Ford reported how fast gas clouds circle the Andromeda Galaxy. Around the Sun, Mercury races far faster than distant Neptune, but in Andromeda the outer clouds kept pace with the inner ones. The mass inside each orbit must keep growing outward, so much of the galaxy's mass lies far out, where little light shines, in a vast unseen halo. Rubin and others found the same in galaxy after galaxy, yet no detector has confirmed a particle of dark matter.

Two rival teams, one led by Saul Perlmutter and one including Adam Riess and Brian Schmidt, measured distant Type Ia supernovae, exploding stars that all peak at almost the same brightness, so their dimness gives their distance. Both expected gravity to be slowing the expansion, but in 1998 both found the distant blasts fainter, and so farther, than expected. Their light had travelled longer than a slowing expansion allows, so the expansion has been speeding up, for the last five or six billion years. Dust, which reddens light as it dims it, was corrected for. The unknown cause was named dark energy.

NASA's WMAP probe and Europe's Planck satellite later mapped the glow's ripples more finely, and the ripples' strength at each size depends on the universe's ingredients. By Planck's count in 2013, ordinary matter, the stuff of every atom, star and planet, is only about a twentieth of the universe. Dark matter is about 27 percent and dark energy about 68, so some 95 percent of the universe is stuff whose nature no one yet knows.
